name: Dagestan
summary_text: Dagestan stands under the national framework of Russia, where the risks facing transgender visitors have sharpened markedly since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these statutes face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and the United States State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The same statutes operate inside Dagestan as they do in every other Russian region.  The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) names the North Caucasus, including Dagestan, as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North Caucasus authorities from 2017 to 2024 involving abduction, torture and extrajudicial killing, and it assesses transgender people and visible advocates as a specific category within that finding rather than treating the region's risk as applying only to sexual orientation.  Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia and separately warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons, singling out the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan. The same advisory states that entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of Interior, a requirement that applies to visitors as well as residents and that can be refused without stated grounds.  David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. For a transgender visitor this means the exposure is not limited to public expression: being recognised as trans in a domestic setting carries the same risk.

name: Ingushetia
summary_text: Ingushetia stands under the framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition is prohibited outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. A 2024 law additionally bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule that also bears on foreign visitors.  Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex", including speech that justifies gender transition. More than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.  Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist. Within 48 hours of the 2023 ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night; arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.  For many transgender Russians emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers, while the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.  At the regional level the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Ingushetia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic regional campaigns between 2017 and 2024, and states that the 2023 "extremist" designation exposes LGBT+ activity to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising, with violence spreading beyond the region.  David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He attests that conditions in the region have deteriorated year on year.  Global Affairs Canada advises avoid all travel to Russia and lists Ingushetia among the republics with frequent terrorist attacks, alongside Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai. The advisory notes surveillance of foreign nationals and states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused; since January 2024, organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as "extremist". The Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas.
